empirical_sources.title: DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025: original infographic and survey instrument
empirical_sources.publication_date: 2025 (year printed on infographic); associated report released September 2025 according to original issuer 2026-01-07 year review; report landing front matter 2025-09-15 is page metadata, not a verified first-publication day
empirical_sources.observation_period: 2025 survey context; instrument asks about current use and the last 3 months. Exact fieldwork start/end dates not available in inspected materials.
empirical_sources.population: Nearly 5,000 technology professionals around the world; infographic also reports over 100 hours of qualitative material. Per-item sample sizes and country weighting not supplied.
empirical_sources.scope: Software-development/technology work; question wording says AI tools, not an isolated LLM-only measure. Not a general population, organization census or hospital clinician sample.
empirical_sources.methodology: Issuer’s cross-sectional self-report survey summary with original questionnaire. Binary current-use question; ordinal frequency over last 3 months. Full 2025 methods section inaccessible at cloud.google.com; do not infer recruitment/weighting from 2024.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The original 2025 DORA infographic reports 90% of technology professionals using AI at work.
claims.denominator: Surveyed technology professionals; exact item n unavailable
claims.locator: One-page infographic, panel 01 Adoption; instrument category Artificial Intelligence, current-use question
claims.qualification: Survey report, not a claim that 90% of global professionals, firms or hospitals deploy LLMs.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The infographic reports 60% of AI users surveyed use AI about half the time or more when encountering a problem/task; original question specifies the last 3 months.
claims.measure: self-reported individual frequency over a retrospective 3-month window
claims.denominator: AI users surveyed; exact item n unavailable
claims.locator: Infographic panel 04 Reflexive use; instrument Artificial Intelligence, frequency question
claims.qualification: Not 60% using daily; not 60% of all developers or firms; not telemetry or longitudinal retention.

limitations: Original publisher empirical summary, not raw microdata replication.
Unknown recruitment, per-item n and weighting in inspected 2025 materials; do not claim probability representativeness.
AI-tools scope is broader than LLM-only coding assistants.
Google Cloud/vendor ecosystem affiliation; D1–D3 and DORA documents are not independent replicated adoption surveys.
2025 observations are historical as of November 2026 and cross the proposed 12-month refresh flag.
No sustained enterprise deployment, hospital documentation penetration or exact Rogers-stage measurement.
empirical_sources.classification: Empirical adoption evidence at individual surveyed-technical-worker level; original instrument verified; methods incomplete

empirical_sources.title: Impact of Generative AI in Software Development, v.2025.2
empirical_sources.publication_date: March 2025 release month stated by issuer’s 2026-01-07 year review; PDF stamped v.2025.2. Exact first-publication day not verified. Landing-page metadata (2025-10-17, updated 2026-04-13) differs from original release and is not substituted for it.
empirical_sources.observation_period: Draws on 2024 DORA survey and September 2024 interviews, not a fresh 2025 prevalence sample.
empirical_sources.population: Underlying 2024 annual survey: nearly 3,000 working professionals, 104 countries (E4). Additional qualitative section: 10 development professionals, approximately 90-minute interviews in September 2024.
empirical_sources.scope: Technical/development work and respondent-reported team incorporation. Not clinician documentation or nationally representative enterprise penetration.
empirical_sources.methodology: Observational self-report survey analyses and qualitative interviews; Bayesian posterior/scenario modeling for team incorporation. Team incorporation defined by respondent estimate of percentage of team work supported by AI in last 3 months. Not a randomized tool-adoption intervention.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The report reiterates that 76% of technologists rely on AI in some part of daily work; this summarizes 2024 data, not new 2025 sampling. E4 gives the unrounded 75.9%.
claims.locator: PDF printed pages 3 and 30; E4 printed page 19
claims.qualification: Daily professional responsibilities is the task context, not an independently measured daily-active-user rate.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The report describes team adoption/incorporation as the respondent-reported percentage of team work supported by AI over the last 3 months.
claims.denominator: Work supported within respondent’s team, not percentage of organizations deployed
claims.locator: PDF printed page 37, note beneath Figure 5
claims.qualification: Neither audited enterprise deployment nor longitudinal sustained use.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The report separately recommends license-allocation and daily-active-user telemetry, and warns these metrics alone do not assess the impact of coding assistants.
claims.measure: proposed measurement guidance, not observed usage result
claims.locator: PDF printed page 41, Code assistant metrics
claims.qualification: Do not turn proposed telemetry into collected local data.

limitations: 2025 publication reuses 2024 evidence; not independent confirmation of E4 or 2025 trend points.
Model associations and strategies are not randomized causal effects; no percentage strategy uplift is admitted to this dossier.
Editorial report wording can overstate causal interpretation; use original methods and uncertainty rather than promotional headings.
Quoted prioritization of integrating AI into applications is strategic intent, not deployed coding-assistant penetration.
empirical_sources.classification: Original 2025 empirical synthesis and measurement framework with explicitly historical underlying data

empirical_sources.title: Managing AI dependency: How students are establishing guardrails with AI
empirical_sources.publisher: DORA authors Andrew Harlan, Kenny Ly, Mindy Tsai
empirical_sources.publication_date: 2026-02-17 (original article front matter, both date and updated)
empirical_sources.observation_period: Eight-month mixed-methods project; exact calendar fieldwork dates not specified in this article.
empirical_sources.population: UC Berkeley students in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, Design and Data Science; article does not provide participant n or a population sampling frame.
empirical_sources.scope: Student academic/coding workflows, not professional company deployment or clinical practice.
empirical_sources.methodology: Original author-reported mixed-methods project using in-depth interviews and survey responses; this article presents qualitative themes and participant quotations, not a penetration estimate.

claims.exact_supported_claim: Participants describe deliberately moderating AI use, attempting problems unaided, alternating assisted/unassisted work and verifying generated code, alongside concerns about dependence and skill development.
claims.denominator: No numerical prevalence claim; bounded student participants
claims.locator: Introduction; Maintaining skill development; Deliberate moderation; Strategies for modulated behavior
claims.qualification: Supports plausible trust/training/verification mechanisms in this study context; does not estimate their prevalence or causal effects in firms.

limitations: Single university and selected fields; no inference to all students, software firms or hospitals.
n, response rate and exact fieldwork dates not reported in inspected article.
Article repeats 2025 DORA statistics and cites other external studies; these repetitions are not new independent evidence and external contents are not admitted.
Recent publication does not make historical cross-referenced statistics fresh.
empirical_sources.classification: 2026 original qualitative empirical mechanism evidence; not an adoption rate

empirical_sources.title: Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024, v.2024.3
empirical_sources.publication_date: 2024 report year; archived PDF v.2024.3. Exact release day not verified; inconsistent landing metadata is not used as the publication date.
empirical_sources.observation_period: 2024 annual survey; exact fieldwork dates not established from inspected sections.
empirical_sources.population: Nearly 3,000 working professionals across industries; respondents from 104 countries. Figure/item denominators vary; no claim all 3,000 answered each item.
empirical_sources.scope: Technology and adjacent roles, with software-task denominators. A respondent’s employer being in Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals does not make the sample one of clinical-documentation users.
empirical_sources.methodology: Original full report inspected at printed pages 19, 91, 97 and 102. Organic recruitment via blogs/email/social media/snowball plus supplementary panels; respondents assigned one of three survey flows (AI, workplace, platform engineering). Randomized survey flows are not randomized AI treatment.

claims.exact_supported_claim: 75.9% of respondents report relying at least in part on AI in one or more daily professional responsibilities.
claims.denominator: DORA respondents for that item; exact n not stated in inspected result section
claims.qualification: Broader AI measure; not an LLM-only daily active metric or enterprise deployment rate.

claims.exact_supported_claim: Among respondents whose job responsibilities include writing code, 74.9% report relying on AI to perform that task at least in part.
claims.denominator: Respondents whose responsibilities include writing code, not all survey respondents, employees or organizations
claims.qualification: Historical 2024 survey result, not sustained authorized enterprise use or an audit.

claims.exact_supported_claim: The report describes nearly 3,000 participants, 104 countries and organic plus supplementary panel recruitment, with three survey flows.
claims.denominator: Overall survey versus item-level denominators must remain distinct
claims.qualification: Do not substitute cumulative research-program participation for this year’s sample.

limitations: Old 2024 evidence; source confidence does not imply current representativeness.
Self-selection, recall, respondent perception and employer/role coverage limits; not a random census of firms.
Survey-flow differences mean overall sample size is not every item’s denominator.
No causal productivity estimate, longitudinal retention or hospital documentation penetration admitted.
empirical_sources.classification: Original historical survey with methods inspected; dependency source for E2, not an independent 2025 replication
